title: Heckler v. Chaney (1985)
summary: Agency refusals to initiate enforcement are presumptively unreviewable under APA § 701(a)(2), subject to statutory constraints and reserved questions.

sections.Parties: Prisoners sentenced to death by lethal injection in Oklahoma and Texas petitioned FDA for enforcement concerning the drugs used in executions. The federal health officials defended FDA’s refusal.
sections.Material Facts: The prisoners alleged that drugs approved for medical treatment were unapproved and potentially unsafe for executions, particularly when administered by untrained personnel. They requested labeling warnings, notices to manufacturers and prisons, seizure procedures, and recommendations for prosecution. FDA questioned its jurisdiction and independently stated that, even assuming authority, it would decline enforcement because of its priorities and the states’ regulation of executions.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment for the government. The D.C. Circuit reversed, finding reviewability and an abuse of discretion, relying in part on an FDA policy statement. The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals on reviewability without deciding whether FDA possessed jurisdiction over the challenged drug uses.
sections.Issue: Was FDA’s refusal to take the requested enforcement steps reviewable under the APA?
sections.Holding: The refusal was presumptively committed to agency discretion under § 701(a)(2), and the FDCA did not supply constraints overcoming that presumption. The Court did not decide the agency-jurisdiction question or a constitutional claim; the prisoners had not presented a colorable constitutional challenge to the refusal.
sections.Reasoning: Enforcement decisions require balancing evidentiary strength, success prospects, resources, and competing priorities, matters for which agencies have institutional advantages. Nonenforcement ordinarily does not itself coerce liberty or property and resembles prosecutorial discretion. The presumption can be rebutted when Congress supplies meaningful enforcement guidelines; Dunlop involved such constraints. The Court found FDA’s cited policy statement vague and inconsistent with its broader reservation of enforcement discretion. It also reserved questions involving abdication of statutory responsibility and other special circumstances described in the notes. Marshall concurred in the judgment but rejected presumptive nonreviewability. He would review deferentially and uphold this refusal on its stated reasons, emphasizing beneficiaries’ concrete interests and traditional limits on corrupt, retaliatory, or otherwise arbitrary decisions. Brennan’s separate concurrence is omitted from the excerpt. The holding protects a category of enforcement choices; it does not declare all agency inaction immune from review.
